source_refs.note: Chapter 1 exercise (PDF 17-21, printed 14-18), solved: each MCQ carries its key worked out from the chapter (the book prints no key), and the short, constructed response and comprehensive questions and numerical problems carry model answers. The printed numerical answers were checked.

blocks.prompt: 1.1 The purpose of study and discoveries in Physics is:

options.text: the development of destructive technology in warfare
development in aesthetics for the world

blocks.explanation: Physics gives the basic principles behind science, technology and engineering; its tools and products have added comforts to our lives (1.1). Its purpose is the betterment of mankind.

blocks.prompt: 1.2 The length of a steel pipe is in between 0.7 m to 0.8 m. Identify from the following, the appropriate instrument to be used for an accuracy of 0.001 m.
blocks.explanation: 0.001 m = 1 mm, the least count of a metre rule, and a metre rule can measure up to 1 m. A screw gauge and Vernier Callipers measure only a few centimetres, and a 10 m tape is not needed for less than 1 m.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The options of 1.2 are printed with the labels (a), (b), (b), (c). They are given here as (a) to (d) in the printed order.

blocks.prompt:
1.3 The diameter of a steel ball is measured using a Vernier callipers and its reading is shown in the figure. What is the diameter of the steel ball?
[Figure: a main scale marked 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 cm; the Vernier scale (marked 5 at its middle) slides on it, with its zero just at the 1.4 cm mark.]
blocks.explanation:
Least count of Vernier Callipers = 0.01 cm.
Main scale reading = 1.4 cm (the Vernier zero is at the 1.4 cm mark).
Vernier reading: the zero line of the Vernier coincides, so 0 × 0.01 cm = 0.00 cm.
Diameter = 1.4 cm + 0.00 cm = 1.40 cm.

blocks.prompt:
1.4 The figure shows the reading on a micrometer screw gauge used to measure diameter of a thin rod. One complete turn of the thimble is 0.50 mm and there are 50 lines on the circular scale. The diameter of the rod is:
[Figure: on the main scale the thimble edge has uncovered the 3 mm mark and the half-millimetre mark after it; the datum line meets the circular scale between the 20 and 15 marks, at 17.]
blocks.explanation:
Least count = pitch / number of circular divisions = 0.50 mm / 50 = 0.01 mm.
Main scale reading = 3.5 mm (3 mm and the next half-millimetre mark are visible).
Circular scale reading = 17 × 0.01 mm = 0.17 mm.
Diameter = 3.5 mm + 0.17 mm = 3.67 mm.

blocks.prompt: 1.5 The number of significant figures of a measurement are defined as:

options.text: they reflect the accuracy of the observation in a measurement
they are the figures which are reasonably reliable
they are the accurately known digits and the first doubtful digit of a measurement

blocks.explanation: Section 1.4 says all three: significant figures are the digits we feel reasonably sure about, they reflect the instrument used (its accuracy), and they are the accurately known digits plus the first doubtful digit.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The options of 1.5 are printed with the labels (a), (c), (d), (c). They are given here as (a) to (d) in the printed order.

blocks.prompt: 1.6 The number of significant figures in the measured mass 2500.0 kg is:
blocks.explanation: In a decimal number, zeros to the right of a significant figure are significant. So 2, 5, 0, 0 and 0 are all significant: five.

blocks.prompt: 1.7 The sum 12 kg + 2.02 kg + 5.1 kg according to appropriate precision is:
blocks.explanation: 12 + 2.02 + 5.1 = 19.12 kg. In addition the answer keeps the smallest number of decimal places; 12 kg has none, so the sum is 19 kg.

blocks.prompt: 1.8 The answer to appropriate precision for the subtraction (1.126-0.97268) is:
blocks.explanation: 1.126 - 0.97268 = 0.15332. 1.126 has the fewest decimal places (three), so the answer is 0.153.

blocks.prompt: 1.9 The answer of the product (2.8723x1.6) to the appropriate number of significant figures is:
blocks.explanation: 2.8723 × 1.6 = 4.59568. In multiplication the answer keeps as many significant figures as the least accurate factor; 1.6 has two, so the answer is 4.6.

blocks.prompt: 1.10 The answer to the mathematical division (45.2 ÷ 6.0) in appropriate number of significant figures is:
blocks.explanation: 45.2 ÷ 6.0 = 7.5333. 6.0 has two significant figures, so the quotient is 7.5.

blocks.prompt: 1.11 The answer to the following mathematical operation 24.4 m x 100 m / 5.0 m to the appropriate number of significant figures is:
blocks.explanation: 24.4 m × 100 m / 5.0 m = 488 m. The least accurate factor 5.0 m has two significant figures, so the answer is 4.9 × 10² m (scientific notation shows the two significant figures clearly).

blocks.prompt: 1.12 The ratio of the dimensions of force and energy is:
blocks.explanation: [F] / [E] = [MLT⁻²] / [ML²T⁻²] = [L⁻¹].

blocks.prompt: 1.13 Identify which pair from the following does not have identical dimensions.

options.text: Moment of inertia and moment of force

blocks.explanation: Moment of inertia (mr²) = [ML²], while moment of force (torque, rF) = [ML²T⁻²]. The other pairs match: work and torque [ML²T⁻²]; angular momentum and Planck's constant [ML²T⁻¹]; impulse and momentum [MLT⁻¹].

blocks.prompt:
1.14 The following figures are of the same Vernier calipers. Figure (1) shows the reading when the jaws are closed while Fig. (2) shows the reading when a solid cylinder is placed between the jaws. The length of the cylinder is:
[Figure (1): with the jaws closed, the Vernier zero lies a little to the right of the main-scale zero (positive zero error). Figure (2): with the cylinder between the jaws, the scale reads about 3.30 cm.]
blocks.explanation:
Fig. (1): the Vernier zero is to the right of the main-scale zero, so the zero error is positive: +0.04 cm (4th Vernier line coincides, L.C. 0.01 cm).
Fig. (2): observed reading = 3.30 cm.
Corrected length = observed reading - zero error = 3.30 cm - 0.04 cm = 3.26 cm.

blocks.prompt: 1.15 The least count of an instrument determines:
blocks.explanation: Section 1.5: the precision of a measurement is determined by the instrument; the smaller the least count, the more precise the measurement. Accuracy depends on the fractional or percentage uncertainty.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The options of 1.15 are printed with the labels (a), (c), (c), (d). They are given here as (a) to (d) in the printed order.

blocks.prompt: 1.16 A measuring tape has been graduated with a minimum scale division of 0.2 cm. The allowed reading using this tape may be:
blocks.explanation: The tape can read only in steps of 0.2 cm: ... 80.4, 80.6, 80.8 cm. Of the options only 80.6 cm (= 403 × 0.2 cm) lies on its scale.

blocks.prompt: 1.1 What are base units and derived units? Give some examples of both these units.
blocks.explanation:
Base units: units of the seven independent base quantities, e.g. metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), ampere (A), kelvin (K), candela (cd), mole (mol).
Derived units: units that depend on base units, e.g. newton (N = kg m s⁻²), joule (J = kg m² s⁻²), watt (W), pascal (Pa), coulomb (C = A s).

blocks.prompt:
1.2 How many significant figures should be retained in the following?
(i) Multiplying or dividing several numbers (ii) Adding or subtracting numbers
blocks.explanation:
(i) Multiplying or dividing: the answer keeps as many significant figures as the factor with the fewest significant figures.
(ii) Adding or subtracting: the answer keeps as many decimal places as the number with the fewest decimal places (here the position of the decimal matters, not the number of significant figures).

blocks.prompt: 1.3 How is the Vernier scale related to the main scale of a Vernier Callipers? What is meant by L.C. of the Vernier Callipers?
blocks.explanation:
The Vernier scale slides along the main scale; its 10 divisions are equal to 9 main-scale divisions (9 mm), so each Vernier division is 0.9 mm, 0.1 mm shorter than a main-scale division.
L.C. (least count) is the smallest length the callipers can measure: L.C. = 1 MSD - 1 VSD = 1 mm/10 = 0.1 mm = 0.01 cm. (beyond the chapter: the Vernier Callipers is not described in this chapter.)

blocks.prompt:
1.4 Write the following numbers in scientific notation.
a) 143.7 (b) 206.4 x 10²
blocks.explanation:
Scientific notation keeps only one non-zero digit left of the decimal.
(a) 143.7 = 1.437 × 10²
(b) 206.4 × 10² = 2.064 × 10⁴

blocks.prompt:
1.5 Write the following numbers using correct prefixes:
(a) 580 x 10² g (b) 0.45 x 10⁻⁶ s
1.6 Kinetic energy of a body of mass m moving with speed v is given by 1/2 mv². What are the dimensions of kinetic energy?
blocks.explanation:
The number ½ has no dimensions.
[K.E.] = [m][v]² = [M][LT⁻¹]² = [ML²T⁻²] (the same as work; unit joule).

blocks.prompt:
1.7 How many significant figures are there in the following measurements?
(i) 37 km (ii) 0.002953 m (iii) 7.50034 cm (iv) 200.0 m
blocks.explanation:
(i) 37 km: 2
(ii) 0.002953 m: 4 (zeros on the left are not significant)
(iii) 7.50034 cm: 6 (zeros between digits are significant)
(iv) 200.0 m: 4 (zeros after a digit in a decimal number are significant)

blocks.prompt: 1.8 Write the dimensions of: (i) Planck's constant (ii) angular velocity
blocks.explanation:
(i) h = E/f: [h] = [ML²T⁻²]/[T⁻¹] = [ML²T⁻¹]
(ii) ω = θ/t, and the angle θ has no dimensions: [ω] = [T⁻¹]

blocks.prompt: 1.1 Why do we find it useful to have two units for the amount of a substance, the kilogram and the mole?
blocks.explanation:
The kilogram measures the mass of a substance (its quantity of matter and inertia); it is used for weighing, force, momentum and energy.
The mole measures the amount of substance as a number of particles (1 mol = 6.02 × 10²³ particles). Chemical reactions take place particle by particle, so the mole is convenient there.
Equal masses of different substances contain different numbers of particles, so both units are needed.

blocks.prompt: 1.2 Three students measured the length of a rod with a scale on which minimum division is 1 mm and recorded as: (i) 0.4235 m (ii) 0.42 m (iii) 0.424 m. Which record is correct and why?
blocks.explanation:
Record (iii) 0.424 m is correct.
The least count is 1 mm = 0.001 m, so a reading should be recorded up to the third decimal place in metres.
0.4235 m claims a precision of 0.1 mm, which this scale cannot give; 0.42 m is only to the nearest centimetre and loses the precision of the scale.

blocks.prompt: 1.3 Why is the kilogram (not the gram), the base unit of mass.
blocks.explanation:
SI is built on the metre, kilogram and second, so that derived units come out without extra factors: 1 N = 1 kg × 1 m s⁻², 1 J = 1 N × 1 m. With the gram, factors such as 10⁻³ would appear in every derived unit.
The gram is also too small for everyday masses, and the standard of mass was made as a 1 kg mass. (beyond the chapter: the chapter does not give this reason.)

blocks.prompt:
1.4 Consider the equation; P = Q + R
If Q and R both have the dimensions of [MLT], what are the dimensions of P? What are the units of P in SI? If the dimensions of Q were different from those of R, could we determine dimensions of P?
blocks.explanation:
Only quantities with the same dimensions can be added, and their sum has the same dimensions: [P] = [MLT].
SI unit of P: kg m s.
If Q and R had different dimensions they could not be added; the equation would be dimensionally wrong (not homogeneous), so the dimensions of P could not be determined.

blocks.prompt:
1.5 What is the least count of a clock if it has:
(a) Hour's hand, minute's hand and second's hand
(b) Hour's hand and minute's hand
blocks.explanation:
Least count = the smallest time the clock can show.
(a) 1 second (the second's hand moves one division = 1 s).
(b) 1 minute (the minute's hand moves one division = 1 min).

blocks.prompt: 1.6 How can the diameter of a round pencil be measured using metre rule with the same accuracy as that of Vernier Callipers? Describe.
blocks.explanation:
Place 10 identical round pencils side by side, touching each other, on a table, and put two wooden blocks at the two ends.
Measure the distance between the blocks with the metre rule (least count 0.1 cm), e.g. 7.5 cm.
Diameter of one pencil = 7.5 cm / 10 = 0.75 cm.
The uncertainty is also divided by 10: 0.1 cm / 10 = 0.01 cm, the same as the least count of Vernier Callipers.

blocks.prompt: 1.7 How would be the readings differ if the screw gauge is used instead of a Vernier Callipers to measure the thickness of a glass plate?
blocks.explanation:
Least count of Vernier Callipers = 0.01 cm; least count of screw gauge = 0.001 cm (0.01 mm), ten times smaller.
So the screw gauge reading has one more significant figure and is more precise, e.g. Vernier: 0.25 cm; screw gauge: 0.253 cm (2.53 mm).
For a thin plate the percentage uncertainty falls from about 4% (0.01/0.25) to about 0.4% (0.001/0.253), so the screw gauge reading is also more accurate.

blocks.prompt:
1.8 Write the correct reading of the length of a solid cylinder as shown in the figure if there is an error of +0.02 cm in the Vernier Callipers.
[Figure: main scale 0 to 4 cm; the zero of the Vernier scale is at the 2.7 cm mark, and the zero line of the Vernier scale coincides with that main-scale line.]
blocks.explanation:
Least count = 0.01 cm.
Main scale reading = 2.7 cm
Vernier scale reading = 0 × 0.01 cm = 0.00 cm (the Vernier zero line coincides)
Observed reading = 2.7 cm + 0.00 cm = 2.70 cm
Zero error = +0.02 cm, so zero correction = -0.02 cm
Correct length = 2.70 cm - 0.02 cm = 2.68 cm

blocks.prompt:
1.9 There are 50 divisions on the circular scale of a screw gauge. If the head (thimble) of the screw is given 10 revolutions, then the spindle advances by 5 mm. There is also zero error as the 2nd division of the circular scale coincides with the datum line and zero of circular scale is below the datum line. What is the thickness of a glass slab as measured by the described screw gauge shown in the figure?
[Figure: main scale marked 0 and 5 mm; the thimble edge has uncovered the 6.5 mm mark; the datum line meets the circular scale at about the 13th division.]
blocks.explanation:
Pitch = distance / revolutions = 5 mm / 10 = 0.5 mm
Least count = pitch / circular divisions = 0.5 mm / 50 = 0.01 mm
Zero error: zero of the circular scale is below the datum line, so the error is positive: +2 × 0.01 mm = +0.02 mm
Main scale reading = 6.5 mm
Circular scale reading = 13 × 0.01 mm = 0.13 mm
Observed reading = 6.5 mm + 0.13 mm = 6.63 mm
Correct thickness = 6.63 mm - 0.02 mm = 6.61 mm
(beyond the chapter: the screw gauge is not described in this chapter.)

blocks.prompt: 1.10 What is meant by a dimensionless quantity? Give one example.
blocks.explanation:
A dimensionless quantity has no dimensions; it is usually a ratio of two quantities with the same dimensions.
Example: plane angle θ = arc length / radius = [L]/[L], so it has no dimensions (its unit, the radian, is dimensionless).

blocks.prompt:
1.11 A student uses a screw gauge to determine the thickness of a sheet of paper. The student folds the paper three times and measures the total thickness of the folded sheet. Assume that there is no zero error in the screw gauge. The reading of screw gauge is shown in the figure. Find the thickness of the sheet.
[Figure: only the 0 mark of the main scale is uncovered; the datum line meets the circular scale (marked 35, 30, 25, 20, 15) at the 25 mark.]
blocks.explanation:
Least count of the screw gauge = 0.01 mm (taken as usual; not printed)
Main scale reading = 0 mm
Circular scale reading = 25 × 0.01 mm = 0.25 mm
Total thickness of folded paper = 0 + 0.25 mm = 0.25 mm
Folding three times doubles the layers each time: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 layers
Thickness of one sheet = 0.25 mm / 8 = 0.031 mm ≈ 0.03 mm (3.1 × 10⁻⁵ m)

blocks.prompt:
1.12 Round off each of the following numbers to 3 significant figures and write your answer in scientific notation.
(a) 0.02055 (b) 4656.5
blocks.explanation:
(a) 0.02055: the digit dropped is 5 and the digit before it (5) is odd, so it is increased: 0.0206 = 2.06 × 10⁻²
(b) 4656.5: deleting digits one by one, 4656.5 → 4656 → 4660 (6 > 5): 4.66 × 10³

blocks.prompt: 1.1 What is meant by uncertainty in a measurement? How the uncertainty in a digital instrument is indicated?
blocks.explanation:
Uncertainty in a measurement:
Every instrument is calibrated to a smallest division, which limits its accuracy. A measurement is taken to the nearest graduation, so every measured quantity has some doubt about its value. This doubt is called uncertainty.
The maximum uncertainty is taken as one smallest division (the least count) of the instrument; this is the absolute uncertainty, e.g. 1 mm for a metre rule graduated in millimetres.
Example: if one edge of a book is at 10.0 cm and the other at 33.5 cm, length = (33.5 ± 0.05) cm - (10.0 ± 0.05) cm = (23.5 ± 0.1) cm, so the true length lies between 23.4 cm and 23.6 cm.
Uncertainty may be recorded as:
Fractional uncertainty = absolute uncertainty / measured value
Percentage uncertainty = (absolute uncertainty / measured value) × 100
Uncertainty in digital instruments:
In a digital scale the uncertainty shows as fluctuation of the last digit. If the last digit fluctuates by 1 or 2, that last digit is written down. If it fluctuates by more than 2, the reading may be affected by some factor such as air currents, and the displayed digit may not be significant.
When the reading is recorded with significant figures, its last (estimated) digit indicates the accuracy of the recorded value, e.g. 3.145 g on an electronic balance means 3.145 ± 0.001 g.

blocks.prompt: 1.2 Differentiate between the terms precision and accuracy with reference to measurement of physical quantities.
blocks.explanation:
Precision depends on the instrument (its absolute uncertainty or least count); accuracy depends on how close the measurement is to the true value (its fractional or percentage uncertainty).
Example (1.5): 25.5 cm by a metre rule (± 0.1 cm, 0.4%) is less precise but more accurate; 0.45 cm by Vernier Callipers (± 0.01 cm, 2%) is more precise but less accurate.

rows: Closeness of a measurement to the exact or accepted value
Expressed by the absolute uncertainty (least count)
Expressed by the fractional or percentage uncertainty
Smaller least count: more precise measurement
Smaller percentage uncertainty: more accurate measurement

blocks.prompt: 1.3 (a) What is meant by significant figures? Write two reasons for using them in measurements. How to find the uncertainty in a timing experiment such as the time period of a simple pendulum?
blocks.explanation:
Significant figures: in any measurement, the accurately known digits and the first estimated (doubtful) digit are called significant figures; they are the digits we feel reasonably sure about.
Two reasons for using them:
1. They show the precision of the instrument used: 3.145 g (electronic balance) is more accurate than 3.1 g (lever balance).
2. They remove the extra, misleading digits a calculator gives, so results are quoted correctly and show their uncertainty (the last digit is uncertain by at least 1 unit).
Uncertainty in a timing experiment (simple pendulum):
1. Time a large number of oscillations, e.g. 20, with a stopwatch of least count 0.1 s: t = 40.6 s.
2. Time period T = 40.6 s / 20 = 2.03 s.
3. Uncertainty in T = least count of the timing device / number of oscillations = 0.1 s / 20 = 0.005 s.
4. So T = 2.030 ± 0.005 s.
Timing many oscillations makes the uncertainty in one period small. If the timing is repeated several times, the mean deviation from the average value is taken as the uncertainty.

blocks.prompt: 1.3 (b) The mass of a solid cylinder is 12.85 g. Its length is 3.35 cm and diameter is 1.25 cm. Find the density of its material expressing the uncertainty in the density.
blocks.explanation:
Given: m = 12.85 g (balance least count 0.01 g), ℓ = 3.35 cm, d = 1.25 cm (Vernier Callipers, least count 0.01 cm)
Required: density ρ with its uncertainty
Volume V = π(d²/4)ℓ = 3.14 × (1.25 cm)² × 3.35 cm / 4 = 4.11 cm³
Density ρ = m/V = 12.85 g / 4.11 cm³ = 3.13 g cm⁻³
%age uncertainty in m = (0.01 g / 12.85 g) × 100 = 0.08%
%age uncertainty in d = (0.01 cm / 1.25 cm) × 100 = 0.8%, and d is squared: 2 × 0.8% = 1.6%
%age uncertainty in ℓ = (0.01 cm / 3.35 cm) × 100 = 0.3%
Total %age uncertainty in ρ = 0.08% + 1.6% + 0.3% ≈ 2%
Absolute uncertainty = 2% of 3.13 g cm⁻³ = 0.06 g cm⁻³
Answer: ρ = (3.13 ± 0.06) g cm⁻³ = (3.13 ± 0.06) × 10³ kg m⁻³

blocks.prompt: 1.4 Explain with examples the writing of physical quantities into their dimensions. Write its two benefits.
blocks.explanation:
Dimensions of a physical quantity show how it is related to the base quantities. The base quantities are written as symbols in square brackets: length [L], mass [M], time [T], electric current [A], temperature [θ].
To write the dimensions of a quantity, write its defining formula and replace each quantity by its dimensions; numbers such as ½ have no dimensions.
Examples:
Speed v = distance/time: [v] = [L]/[T] = [LT⁻¹]
Acceleration a = Δv/Δt: [a] = [LT⁻¹]/[T] = [LT⁻²]
Force F = ma: [F] = [M][LT⁻²] = [MLT⁻²]
Work W = Fd: [W] = [MLT⁻²][L] = [ML²T⁻²]
Density ρ = m/V: [ρ] = [M]/[L³] = [ML⁻³]
Two benefits:
1. Checking the homogeneity (correctness) of an equation: the dimensions on both sides must be the same, e.g. S = ½at² gives [L] = [LT⁻²][T²] = [L], so it is dimensionally correct.
2. Deriving a formula: if we know the quantities on which a quantity depends, we can find the form of the formula, e.g. F = (constant) mv²/r for centripetal force (Example 1.4).
(The method cannot give the value of a numerical constant; that comes from experiment.)

blocks.prompt:
1.5 Check the homogeneity of the relation:
v = √(T × ℓ / m)
where v is the speed of transverse wave on a stretched string of tension T, length ℓ and mass m.
blocks.explanation:
Dimensions of the left side: [v] = [LT⁻¹]
Tension is a force: [T] = [MLT⁻²]; [ℓ] = [L]; [m] = [M]
Dimensions of the right side = √([MLT⁻²][L] / [M]) = √[L²T⁻²] = [LT⁻¹]
Both sides have the dimensions [LT⁻¹], so the relation is homogeneous (dimensionally correct).

blocks.prompt: 1.1 Astronomers usually measure astronomical distances in light years. One light year is the distance that light travels in one year. If speed of light is 3 x 10⁸ m s⁻¹, what is one light year in metres? (Ans: 9.5x10¹⁵ m)
blocks.explanation:
Given: c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, t = 1 year
Required: distance S
t = 365 × 24 × 60 × 60 s = 3.15 × 10⁷ s
S = c × t
S = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ × 3.15 × 10⁷ s
S = 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m ≈ 9.5 × 10¹⁵ m
This agrees with the book's answer.

blocks.prompt:
1.2 Write the estimated answer of the following in standard form.
(a) How many seconds are there in 1 year?
(b) How many years are in 1 second?
(Ans: (a) 3.2 x 10⁷ s (b) 3.1 x 10⁻⁸ years)
blocks.explanation:
(a) 1 year = 365 × 24 × 60 × 60 s = 31 536 000 s ≈ 3.2 × 10⁷ s
(b) 1 s = 1 / (3.2 × 10⁷) year = 3.1 × 10⁻⁸ year
Both agree with the book's answers (with the exact value 3.15 × 10⁷ s, (b) is 3.2 × 10⁻⁸ year; the book uses the estimate of (a)).

blocks.prompt: 1.3 The length and width of a rectangular plate are measured to be 18.3 cm and 14.60 cm, respectively. Find the area of the plate and state the answer to correct number of significant figures. (Ans: 267 cm²)
blocks.explanation:
Given: length ℓ = 18.3 cm (3 significant figures), width b = 14.60 cm (4 significant figures)
Required: area A
A = ℓ × b = 18.3 cm × 14.60 cm = 267.18 cm²
The least accurate factor 18.3 cm has three significant figures, so
A = 267 cm²
This agrees with the book's answer.

blocks.prompt:
1.4 Find the sum of the masses given in kg up to appropriate precision:
(i) 3.197 (ii) 0.068 (iii) 13.9 (iv) 3.28 (Ans: 20.4 kg)
blocks.explanation:
Sum = 3.197 kg + 0.068 kg + 13.9 kg + 3.28 kg = 20.445 kg
13.9 kg has the fewest decimal places (one), so the sum is rounded to one decimal place:
20.445 → 20.44 → 20.4 kg
This agrees with the book's answer.

blocks.prompt: 1.5 The diameter and length of a metal cylinder measured with the help of a Vernier Callipers of least count 0.01 cm are 1.22 cm and 5.35 cm respectively. Calculate its volume and uncertainty in it. (Ans: 6.2 ± 0.1 cm³)
blocks.explanation:
Given: d = 1.22 cm, ℓ = 5.35 cm, least count = 0.01 cm
Required: volume V and its uncertainty
V = π(d²/4)ℓ = 3.14 × (1.22 cm)² × 5.35 cm / 4 = 6.25 cm³
%age uncertainty in d = (0.01 cm / 1.22 cm) × 100 = 0.82%; for d²: 2 × 0.82% = 1.64%
%age uncertainty in ℓ = (0.01 cm / 5.35 cm) × 100 = 0.19%
Total %age uncertainty in V = 1.64% + 0.19% = 1.83%
Absolute uncertainty = 1.83% of 6.25 cm³ = 0.11 cm³ ≈ 0.1 cm³ (one significant figure)
The volume is then rounded to the place of the uncertainty: 6.25 → 6.2 (the dropped 5 follows an even digit)
V = 6.2 ± 0.1 cm³
This agrees with the book's answer.

blocks.prompt: 1.6 Show that the expression vf² - vi² = 2aS is dimensionally correct, where vi is the initial velocity, a is the acceleration and vf is the velocity after covering a distance S.
blocks.explanation:
Left side: [vf²] - [vi²]; both terms have the same dimensions [LT⁻¹]² = [L²T⁻²]
Right side: the number 2 has no dimensions; [a][S] = [LT⁻²][L] = [L²T⁻²]
Both sides have the dimensions [L²T⁻²], so the expression is dimensionally correct.

blocks.prompt: 1.7 Show that the famous "Einstein equation" E = mc² is dimensionally consistent.
blocks.explanation:
Left side: E is energy (work): [E] = [ML²T⁻²]
Right side: [m][c]² = [M][LT⁻¹]² = [ML²T⁻²]
Both sides have the same dimensions, so E = mc² is dimensionally consistent.

blocks.prompt:
1.8 Derive a formula for the time period of a simple pendulum using dimensional analysis. The various possible factors on which the time period T may depend are:
(i) length of the pendulum ℓ
(ii) mass of the bob m
(iii) angle θ which the thread makes with the vertical
(iv) accelerates due to gravity g.
(Ans: T = Constant √(ℓ/g))
blocks.explanation:
The angle θ has no dimensions, so its effect goes into the constant and cannot be found by this method.
Let T = (constant) ℓᵃ mᵇ gᶜ ...... (i)
Writing dimensions (the constant has none):
[T] = [L]ᵃ [M]ᵇ [LT⁻²]ᶜ
[M⁰L⁰T¹] = [Mᵇ Lᵃ⁺ᶜ T⁻²ᶜ]
Comparing the powers:
M: b = 0
T: -2c = 1, so c = -½
